Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 4, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 3):

Madaniyya (Medinan), containing sixteen thousand and thirty letters, three thousand seven hundred and forty-five words and one hundred, and seventy-six verses.

On the authority of Abu Umama, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Nisa', it is as if he has given charity to every believer who has inherited an inheritance, and he is given a reward like one who has freed a slave, and he is free from shirk, and he is among those whom Allah may pardon." [Majma' al-Bayan: 3/5.] [225]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾ — meaning Adam — ﴿and created from it its mate﴾ — meaning Eve. Its parallel is in Surat al-A'raf and al-Zumar. ﴿And dispersed from the two of them many men and women.﴾ *Batha* means he spread and made manifest. ﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another﴾ — you ask one another by Him. The people of Kufa lightened it (*tasa'alun*) by dropping one of the two *ta'*s, as a lightening, like His saying: ﴿and do not cooperate﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 2] and similar. ﴿And the wombs.﴾

The common reading is with the accusative (*nasb*), meaning: ﴿and fear the wombs, lest you sever them.﴾

Al-Nakha'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talha ibn Musarrif, Qatada, al-A'mash and Hamza read it in the genitive (*khafd*), meaning *wa-bil-arham* (and by the wombs), as one says: "I ask you by Allah and the Merciful," and "I adjure you by Allah and the Merciful." The first reading is more correct and more eloquent, because the Arabs do not coordinate an apparent noun with a pronoun governed by a preposition, unless they repeat the governing particle, saying: "I passed by him and by Zayd," or they put it in the accusative, as in the words of the poet:

"O people, what is wrong with me and Abu Dhu'ayb?"

However, it is permissible with the aforementioned construction, and it occurs in poetry. The poet said:

"Today you have come near to satirizing us and insulting us... go, what have you to do with the days, [which are] a wonder?" [Sharh al-Radi 'ala al-Kafiya: 2/336; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/14.]

Al-Farra' recited for one of the Ansar:

"We hang our swords among the like of pillars, and between them and the ankle is a ... (mahwa / ghawt) of nafanif." [Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/300; al-Qurtubi: 5/3, where it reads *mahwa* instead of *ghawt*.]

Abdullah ibn Yazid al-Muqri' read ﴿wal-arhamu﴾ in the nominative, as if he intended the sentence to be complete at His saying ﴿you ask one another by Him﴾, and then began anew, as one says: "Zayd should be honoured." It may also be an exhortation (*igra'*), since the Arabs put the one being urged in the nominative.

Al-Farra' recited:

"Where are the people among whom is 'Umayr, and the likes of 'Umayr, and among them al-Saffah,
worthy of meeting when the champion of valour says: 'The weapons! The weapons!'" [Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/208; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/6.]

﴿Indeed Allah is ever watchful over you﴾ — i.e., a guardian. It is said: it means *fa'il* (one who watches).

﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ — the verse.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning a man from Ghatafan who had much property belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the orphan reached maturity he demanded the property, but his uncle refused him, so they went to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. When the uncle heard it, he said: "We obey Allah and we obey the Messenger; we seek refuge in Allah from the great sin," and he handed over his property to him.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul and obeys his Lord in this way, he will enter his abode," meaning his Paradise. When the young man received his property, he spent it in the way of Allah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The reward remains and the burden remains."

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we understand that the reward remains, but how does the burden remain, when he spent it in the way of Allah?"

He said: "The reward remains for the boy, and the burden remains upon his father." And ﴿give﴾ is an address to the guardians and executors of orphans. [Al-Qurtubi: 5/8; Asbab al-Nuzul: 94, with variation in wording.] [227]

As for His saying, ﴿the orphans﴾: they are no longer orphans after reaching maturity, but this is figurative usage, like His saying: ﴿and the sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾ [Surat al-A'raf: 120]. There were no sorcerers with the prostration, but they were named by what they had been before prostrating.

His saying: ﴿give the orphans their property﴾ means: those who were orphans, when they reach maturity ﴿and you perceive in them maturity of judgement﴾. Its parallel is: ﴿and test the orphans﴾ [Surat al-Nisa': 6]. ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ means: do not substitute their unlawful property that is upon you for your lawful property that is for you. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿The bad and the good are not equal﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 100].

They differed concerning the meaning and manner of this interpretation:

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: The guardians of orphans and their executors would take the good and choice from the orphans' property and put in its place the inferior and base, so one of them might take a fat sheep from the orphan's property and put in its place a lean sheep, and take a good dirham and throw in its place a counterfeit, and say: "A dirham for a dirham." That is their substitution, and Allah the Exalted forbade it.

Ata': "Do not profit at the expense of your orphan who is in your charge, while he is weak and young."

Ibn Zayd: The people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance to women and children, and the eldest would take the inheritance.

Ibn Zayd also said: ﴿and you desire to marry them, and the weak among the children﴾ — they did not give them any share of the inheritance; so their share of the inheritance is good, and this which they took is bad.

Mujahid and Badhan: "Do not hasten the unlawful provision before the lawful comes to you."

﴿And do not devour their property along with your property﴾ — i.e., together with your property, like His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers to Allah?﴾ [Surat Al 'Imran: 52; Surat al-Saff: 14].

Al-Mufaddal recited Salama ibn al-Kharashib al-Ansari:

"They close the doors of the tents with lean [horses] towards ... firmly fastened tendons (ankles/nawasir)." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/10; Lisan al-'Arab: 4/23.]

That is, together with *'unun*.

﴿Indeed it is a great sin﴾ — i.e., a grave wrong. In it there are three dialects: the common reading is *huban* with a *damma*, and it is the dialect of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the people of the Hijaz, as shown by what Abu 'Ubayd related from 'Abbad ibn 'Abbad, from Wasil, the client of Ibn 'Uyayna, who said: I said to Ibn Sirin: "How is this word read: *innahu kana hauban* or *haubā*?" He said: Abu Ayyub wished to divorce Umm Ayyub, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "The divorce of Umm Ayyub is a sin (*hawb*)." [al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 25/136.] [228]

al-Hasan read *haubā* with a fatha on the *ha'*, which is the dialect of Tamim.

[Muqatil said: the dialect of the Abyssinians.] [Addition from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/10.]

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read *hābā* as a verbal noun, like *al-qāl*, and it may be a noun like *al-rād* and *al-nār*. It is said that the sin is *hawb* and *hāb*, and so for the plural; it is both verbal noun and noun. It is said: *hāba yahūbu hawban* and *hawban* and *hibāyatan* when one sins.

Abu Mu'adh said: We alighted at a place near a city, and a man threw a small stone [and it was said to him]: "O pilgrim, do not kill it, lest you incur a sin (*hawb*); it does not harm." From this the killer is called *hā'ib*. Al-Farra' related it from the Banu Asad.

Umayya ibn al-Askan al-Laythi, whose son had emigrated without his permission, said:

"Even if two emigrants surround him that morning, they have erred and sinned (*hābā*)."
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/306.]

Another said:

"Bite on your molars, the shrewd one, so he does not blame nor sin (*yahūb*)."
[al-Fa'iq li-l-Zamakhshari: 2/180.]

Another said:

"And the son of her son from us and from you, and her husband Khuzayma, and the wombs, the distress of her sin (*hawbihā*)."
[Lisan al-'Arab: 2/202.]

That is, its sin is severe.

Another said:

"Do not weep for me, nor lament with the speech of sin; indeed sin is a grave wrong (*hawb*)."
[Tarikh Dimashq: 63/173.]

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with regard to the orphans﴾ — the verse. The exegetes differed concerning its revelation and interpretation. Some of them said: its meaning is: "And if you fear that you will not be just, O guardians of orphans, regarding them, when you marry them, then marry others besides them from the women whom Allah has made lawful to you."

Al-Zuhri related from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, who said: I asked her about the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with regard to the orphans﴾. She said: "O son of my brother, it refers to the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian, who desires her wealth and beauty and wishes to marry her for less than her dowry. They were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly towards them in completing the dowry, and they were ordered to marry other women besides them."

al-Hasan said: A man of Madina would have orphans in his care, and among them were some whom it was lawful for him to marry, but he would say to her: "I will not let anyone enter my property," out of dislike that a stranger should enter and share in their wealth. So he might marry them for the sake of their wealth, and [marry] one whom he does not find pleasing, then he forgets their companionship and waits for them to die so that he may inherit from them. Allah the Mighty and Majestic condemned that, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.

'Ikrima: A man of Quraysh would marry ten women, or more or less. When he became unable to meet the expenses of his wives, he would seize the property of his orphan ward in his care and spend it. So it was said to them: "Refrain from women, and do not exceed four, lest it lead you to take the property of orphans." This is the report of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the sense of the report of 'Ata' from him.

Others said: They would scruple and feel sinful regarding the property of orphans, and would be lax regarding women, not limiting themselves regarding them, and would marry as many as they wished, so that they were sometimes just and sometimes not. When they asked about the matter of the orphans' property, Allah revealed ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, and He also revealed this verse: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with regard to the orphans﴾, meaning: just as you fear not being just with the orphans and it preoccupies you, so likewise fear regarding women that you will not be just to them, and do not marry more than you can keep and fulfil their rights, for women are like the orphan in weakness and helplessness. How is it that you are conscientious towards Allah the Mighty and Majestic in one matter, yet disobey Him in its like? This is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, and the report of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

al-Hasan also said: They scrupled over marrying orphans as they scrupled over their property, so Allah revealed this verse, and granted leniency regarding them and restricted them to a number. So it is incumbent upon you to be just regarding them. If you fear, O guardians, regarding the orphans whose guardianship you hold, that you will not act justly, then marry them, but do not exceed four, so that you may be just; and if you fear that you will not be just regarding them, then one.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The men were restricted to four women because of the orphans.

Mujahid: its meaning is: if you scrupulously avoid the guardianship of orphans, then [scrupulously avoid] their property out of faith and belief; likewise be scrupulous about adultery, and marry lawful women in a good marriage. Then He specified for them a limited number, whereas they used to marry as many as they wished without any number. So Allah revealed ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾, i.e., that you will not be just.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read *tuqsitū* with a fatha on the *ta'*, which is also from justice.

al-Zajjaj said: *qasata* and *aqsata* are one; however, the more eloquent is *aqsata* when he is just, and *qasata* when he is unjust. If the reading of Ibrahim is taken to mean injustice, and *lā* is considered superfluous, the sentence is sound. *Al-yatama* is the plural of male orphans.

﴿So marry﴾ — *mā*.

Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ayla read *man* (مَن), because *mā* is for what does not reason and *man* for what reasons. Whoever reads *mā* has two aspects:

First: that it refers to the act, not the person, its meaning being: "marry the marriage which is lawful to you from women." This is like saying: "Take from my companion what you wish, and the brothers," making *mā* mean *man*. The Arabs interchange *mā* with *man* and *man* with *mā*.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿By the heaven and He who built it﴾ [Surat al-Shams: 5] and its like, and He said: ﴿Of them is one who walks on his belly﴾ [Surat al-Nur: 45].

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' related that the people of Makka, when they heard thunder, said: "Glory to Him whom the thunder glorifies." And Allah said: ﴿Pharaoh said: And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [Surat al-Shu'ara': 23].

﴿Good for you of women, two, three, or four﴾ — *tāba*, *ḥalla lakum min al-nisā'*.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Juhdari and al-A'mash read *tāba* with *imāla* (inclination of the vowel), and in the codex of Ubayy it is written *ṭayyib* with a *yā'*, which is evidence of *imāla*.

*Mathnā wa-thulātha wa-rubā'* are inflected away from two, three and four, and therefore are not declined. There are dialect forms: *muwaḥḥad, mathnā, muthallath, mirba'*, and *aḥād, thanā', thulātha, rubā'*, and *aḥad, thunā, thulth, rub'*, like *'Umar* and *Zufar*.

Likewise al-Nakha'i read this verse. No formation beyond four is used except one line from al-Kumayt:

"They did not ask you to pause until you had struck, above the men, qualities of ten (*'ishār*)."
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/316.]

That is, you struck ten.

They said: Here it means [*law* for affirmation] [The apparent reading is so.], as in His saying: ﴿I admonish you with one thing: that you stand up for Allah in pairs and singly﴾ [Surat Saba': 46], and His saying: ﴿Possessors of wings, two, three, and four﴾ [Surat Fatir: 1]. This is the consensus of the community, and the particular privileges of the Prophet (ﷺ) are not shared.

al-Kalbi, from Khumaisa bint al-Shamardal: Qays ibn al-Harith related to her that he had eight free wives. He said: When this verse was revealed, I said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has revealed to you the prohibition of marrying free women beyond four, and I have eight wives." He said: "Divorce four and keep four." He said: I returned to my house and began to say to the wife who had not borne me children: "O so-and-so, go back," and to the wife who had borne children: "O so-and-so, come forward." Then the one he divorced would say: "I adjure you by Allah and by affection." He said: So I divorced four and kept four. [Abridged, Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/628, hadith 1952.]

﴿And if you fear﴾ — you feared, and it is said: you knew — ﴿that you will not act justly﴾ among the four — ﴿then one﴾.

The common reading is with the accusative (*naṣb*).

al-Hasan, al-Juhdari and Abu Ja'far read *wāḥidatun* with the nominative, meaning: let one suffice you, i.e., one that is sufficient, like His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and if there are not two men, then a man and two women﴾ [Surat al-Baqara: 282].

﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾ — meaning the slave-girls and concubines, because you are not bound towards them by the rights and duties that bind you in regard to marriage; there is no division of time for you among them, and no limit upon you regarding their number. Mention of "right hands" is an explanation of the sense: *aw mā malakat*.

Some scholars of meaning said: *aw mā malakat aymānukum* means: that which your divisions (*aqsām*) take effect upon; he took it from the oath of swearing, not the oath of the limb, and he argued by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no vow in disobedience to Allah, nor in what the son of Adam does not possess." [al-Sunan al-Kubra: 10/33; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/711.] [230]

﴿That is nearer﴾ — closer — ﴿that you will not commit excess (*ta'ūlū*)﴾.

From Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, from 'A'isha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿That is nearer that you will not commit excess﴾, he said: "That you will not act unjustly." [Fath al-Qadir: 1/424.] [231]

Hisham ibn 'Urwa also related from 'A'isha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿That is nearer that you will not commit excess﴾ — that you will not deviate. Most exegetes hold this view.

Muqatil said: It is the dialect of Jurhum; it is said: *mīzān 'ā'il*, meaning a leaning scale. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to the people of Kufa concerning something they had reproached him for: "I am not a scale that leans (*lā u'ūl*)."

'Ikrima recited for Abu Talib:

"With a scale of truth that does not shortchange a grain, having a witness from itself, not leaning."
[Lisan al-'Arab: 11/489; al-Sihah of al-Jawhari: 5/1777.]

Mujahid said: That is nearer that you will not go astray. Al-Farra' and al-Asamm said: that you will not exceed what Allah has obligated upon you; the root of *'awl* is excess, and from it comes *'awl al-farā'id* (the increase in shares of inheritance). al-Shafi'i said: that you will not have many dependants. No one said this except him. It is said: *a'āla yu'īlu* when his dependants increase. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/22, which mentions that al-Daraqutni and Jabir ibn Yazid adopted this opinion.]

Abu Hatim said: [al-Shafi'i] was more knowledgeable in the language of the Arabs than we are, and perhaps this is a dialect.

al-Tha'labi said: Our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: I asked Abu 'Amr al-Duri about this, and he was an unchallenged imam in language. He said: It is the dialect of Himyar.

And he recited:

"Indeed death seizes every living being, without doubt, even if he walks [with many] and has many dependants (*'ālā*)."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/22.]

That is, his flocks and dependants increased.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: The Arab tongues have multiplied so much that I fear I will take a solecism from a speaker of error.

Talha ibn Musarrif read *allā ta'ūlū* (*ta'ūlū*, from *i'āla*), which is the strength of al-Shafi'i's opinion. Some read *allā ta'ūlū* from *al-'ayla*, i.e., not to become poor.

The poet said:

"The poor man does not know when he will become wealthy, and the wealthy man does not know when he will become poor (*yu'īl*)."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/106.]

Tawus read *lā ta'ūlū*, from *al-'illa* (the ailment).

Bashir ibn Nahik related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has two wives and inclines towards one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of him leaning." [Sunan Abi Dawud: 1/473; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/341.] [232]

﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾ (*nihla*).

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 4, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Kalbi and a group of scholars said: this is addressed to the guardians (awliya'). The guardian of a woman, when he married her to a stranger, would carry her to him on a camel and would give her nothing of her dowry (mahr). If she was among her own tribe, he would not give her any of her dowry, little or much. If she was a stranger, he would carry her on a camel to her husband and give her nothing beyond that camel.

For this reason they used to say to a man who had a daughter born to him: "Congratulations on the nafijah [[al-nafijah: one who enlarges her father's wealth; cited in al-Sihah, 1/345.]]." They meant that he takes her dowry in camels and adds them to his camels, so he swells them (yanfajuha), that is, he enlarges and increases them.

Some women said of their husband:
"He does not take the bribe (hulwan) from his daughters."
She meant: he does not do what others do. So God, Mighty and Majestic, forbade them from this and commanded them to give the right (haqq) to its people.

Al-Hadrami said: the guardians of women used to give one man's sister in exchange for the other man giving his sister, with no dowry between them. They were forbidden from this, and God commanded them to name the dowry and to specify the mahr at the contract.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no shighar (exchange-marriage) in Islam." [[Sahih Muslim: 4/139; Musnad Ahmad: 4/441.]] [233]

Others said: the address is to the husbands, who were commanded to give their wives their dowries, which are the price of their private parts (furuj). This view is more sound and clearer in the apparent meaning of the verse, and closer to it, because God addressed the marrying parties in what precedes it, and this is the basic form of address. The word sadaqat (dowries) is the plural of sadaqah, pronounced with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal in the plural form; this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Tamim. Some say sadaqah with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal. When they pluralize it they say sadaqat with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal, and sadaqat with a damma on both, like zulmah and zulumat. Zulumat has as its counterpart al-mathulat (plural of mathulah), the dialect of Tamim being mathulah and mathulat, and mathulat with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha', its singular being mathulah, in the plural form, the dialect of the Hijaz.

Nihlatan: Qatadah said: an obligatory duty (fari'dah wajibah). Ibn Juraij and Ibn Zayd said: a specified duty (fari'dah musammah). Abu 'Ubayd said: a nihlah cannot be specified and known. Al-Kalbi said: a gift and a grant. Abu 'Ubaydah said: from a willing soul (an tayyib nafs). Al-Zajjaj said: as a religious obligation (tadayyun). In it there are two dialects: nihlah and nahlah. Its origin is from giving, and it is in the accusative as a specification (tafsir), and it was said it is an infinitive (masdar).

Marthad ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The most worthy of conditions to be fulfilled is that by which you have made the private parts lawful for you." [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/144; Musnad Abi Ya'la: 2/291.]] [234]

And from Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ziyad ibn Suhayb, from his father, from his grandfather Suhayb, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes on a debt while intending not to repay it will meet God, Mighty and Majestic, as a thief; and whoever gives a woman a dowry while intending not to pay it to her will meet God, Mighty and Majestic, as an adulterer." [[al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 8/35; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/322, no. 44724.]] [235]

﴿And if they are pleased to give you of it something willingly﴾ — meaning: if their souls are content to give you something of that, and they gift it to you. The verb is thus shifted from the souls to their owners, so the soul is an explicit specification (tamyiz). That is why "nafs" is singular, as one says: "He was constricted by it in measure (dharʿan)" and "his eye was cooled by it," and God says: ﴿and he was distressed on their account, and his heart was constricted﴾ [[Surah al-'Ankabut: 33.]].

Some grammarians of Kufa said: its wording is singular but its meaning is plural, and the Arabs do this often.

The poet said:
"Therein are the carcasses of the exhausted; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are hard."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/325.]]

Another said:
"In your throats there is a bone, and we have been choked by it."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/325.]]

Some grammarians of Basra said:
"When the night draws near, the lover's desire ..."
[[al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 10/225.]]
Here al-hawa (desire) is a masdar, and masdars are not pluralized.

﴿Then eat it﴾ means: take it and accept it. ﴿with ease and pleasure﴾ (hanian mariyan). Al-Hadrami said: some people used to feel sinful about a man taking back anything of what he had given to his wife, so God said: ﴿And if they are pleased to give you of it something willingly﴾, without compulsion or deception, ﴿then eat it with ease and pleasure﴾, meaning: pleasant and good. It is derived from the word hanna't al-ba'ir (the mange-treatment of a camel), when one treats it with tar for mange. The meaning is: eat it, healing and free from harm. Hana'ani al-ta'am yahnini (food made me comfortable) with the fatha on the nun in the past tense and kasra in the future tense, yahniini and yahnani, which is the opposite and is rare. The masdar of both is hana'un; one says: hana'ani and mara'ani without the alif. When they use them separately they say amra'ani with an alif. It was also said: al-hanii is the good enjoyment that nothing disturbs, and al-mari' is one whose outcome is praised, complete in digestion, harmless and not injurious. The meaning is: you will not fear in this world any demand, nor in the Hereafter any consequence.

This is supported by what Jawaybir narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he was asked about this verse, ﴿And if they are pleased to give you of it something willingly﴾, and he said: "If she gives her husband a gift willingly, not under compulsion, no authority will judge against you concerning it, and God will not hold you accountable for it in the Hereafter." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/27.]] [236]

Ibrahim ibn 'Isa narrated from 'Ali ibn 'Ali, from Abu Hamzah, who said: "hanian" means there is no sin in it, "mari'an" means there is no reckoning for it in the Hereafter.

Shu'bah narrated from 'Ali, who said: "If one of you is afflicted with something, let him ask his wife for three dirhams of her dowry, then buy honey with it, and drink it with rainwater; then God will gather for him the pleasant and wholesome, the healing, and the blessed water."

﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth which God has made for you a means of support﴾ — the verse.

They differed about who these foolish ones are.

Some people said: they are the women.

Al-Hadrami said: a man deliberately gave his wealth to his wife, and she placed it in other than what is right, so God revealed this verse.

Mujahid said: He forbade men from giving women their wealth, and he specified the foolish ones as being those who were wives, or were daughters, or were mothers.

Jawaybir narrated from al-Dahhak: women are among the most foolish of the foolish. This interpretation is supported by what 'Ali ibn Zayd narrated from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the Fire was created only for the foolish," he said it three times, "and indeed the foolish are women, except a woman who obeys her guardian." [[We have not found this hadith in this wording.]] [237]

Aban narrated from Ibn 'Ayyash, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: a black woman, bold in speech and sharp-tongued, came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "May my father and mother be sacrificed for you, O Messenger of God, say something good about us once, for it has reached me that you say all kinds of evil about us." He said: "What did you say to us?" She said: "You called us the foolish in His Book and you called us the deficient." He said: "Is it not enough deficiency that each of you leaves prayer for five days every month? Does it not suffice one of you that when she becomes pregnant she has the reward of one who guards the frontier in the path of God, and when she gives birth she is like one who is rolling in his blood in the path of God, and when she nurses, for every sip she has the reward of freeing a slave from the descendants of Isma'il, and when she stays awake, for every wakeful night she has the reward of freeing a slave from the descendants of Isma'il? That belongs to the believing women who are humble, patient, and who do not deny their husbands." [[238]] The black woman said: "How great a virtue, were it not for the condition that follows it." [[Majma' al-Bayan: 3/18.]]

'Asim narrated from Muriq, who said: a woman with a dignified bearing passed by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and Ibn 'Umar said to her: ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth﴾. Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah said: accustom your women, for they are foolish; if a woman obeys you, she will ruin you.

Others said: they are the children, and this is the narration of 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Zuhri, Abu Malik, and Ibn [...] said: Do not give your foolish child your wealth, which is your support after God, lest he ruin it. Some of them said: they are the women and the boys. Al-Hasan said: it means your foolish wife and your foolish son.

Qatadah: God commanded that this wealth be stored and its treasuries well kept, and that it not be possessed by a foolish woman or a foolish boy, lest he squander it. God said: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 188.]].

'Ubayd narrated from al-Dahhak: Do not give your women and your children your wealth, lest they become masters over you.

Ibn 'Abbas: Do not turn to the wealth which God has entrusted to you and made a means of living for you, and give it to your wife and sons, so that they become those who stand over you, then you look at what is in their hands. Rather, keep and improve it, and be the one who spends upon them in their clothing, their provision, and their maintenance.

Al-Kalbi: If a man knows that his wife is foolish and corrupt, and that his son is foolish and corrupt, he should not empower either of them over his wealth to ruin it.

Al-Suddi said: Do not give a woman her property until she marries, even if she reads the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an, and do not give a boy his property until he reaches puberty.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah said: it refers to the property of an orphan that is in your keeping. It means: do not give it to him, and spend upon him until he reaches maturity.

If it is said, on this view: how did He attribute the wealth to the guardians, saying ﴿your wealth﴾, when it is the wealth of the foolish? It is said: He attributed it to them because it is the kind of thing God made as wealth for people, like His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from yourselves, grievous to him is what you suffer﴾ [[Surah al-Tawbah: 128.]], and His saying: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 54.]], He returns it to the kind, that is, the kind which is your kind.

Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: it was attributed to the guardians because they are its custodians and managers. The foolish one, whom it is not permitted for his guardian to give his wealth, is one who deserves restriction (hajr) because of squandering his wealth, ruining it, and mismanaging it.

Al-Sha'bi narrated from Abu Burdah, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: Three people call upon God and He does not answer them: a man whose wife had a bad character and he did not divorce her; a man who had a debt owed to him by another man and did not call witnesses against him; and a man who gave his wealth to a foolish person, and God has said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth﴾, meaning: those ignorant of the place of right.

﴿Your wealth which﴾ (amwalakum al-lati).
Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i recited: al-lati, and both have the same meaning.

And he recited:
"Of the lawati and the lati and the lati, they claimed that I had grown old for my pleasure."
[[Lisan al-'Arab: 15/239.]]
So he combined three dialects.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say in the plural of women: al-lati, more often than you say al-lati; and they say in the plural of wealth and all other things: al-lati, more often than they say al-lati. Both are permissible.

﴿Which God has made for you a means of support (qiyaman)﴾. Ibn 'Umar recited (qawaman) with a waw and a fatha on the qaf, like al-dawam. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited (qiwaman) with a kasra on the qaf, as a verb, because the original is with a waw.

Al-Kisa'i said: both are dialects and have the same meaning. Abu Hatim distinguished between them, saying: al-qiwam with a kasra is the means of sustenance (al-mulak), and al-qawam with a fatha is the stature of the body.

Al-A'raj and Nafi' recited (qayyiman) with a kasra on the qaf. The rest recited (qiyaman), and its origin is qiwaman, the waw changed into a ya' because of the kasra before it, like siyam and niyam. All of them are the foundation of the matter and what a person depends upon. It is said: so-and-so is the one who sustains his household. Here it means the means by which your living is sustained.

Al-Dahhak said: by it the Hajj, jihad, and all righteous deeds are established, and it is the ransom of necks from the Fire.

Some of them said: your wealth by which you stand up.

﴿And provide for them from it and clothe them﴾, that is: feed them, and clothe those whose provision is obligatory upon you and whose maintenance you are bound to. Provision from God, Mighty and Majestic, is an unlimited gift; and from people it is a fixed wage tied to a specified time. One says: so-and-so provided for his dependents such-and-such, meaning he gave them a regular allowance. He said "from it" (fiha), not "from it" (minha), because he intended to make provision for them within it, as if He obligated them to do so.

﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾: a good promise. 'Ata' said: "A kind word": when you profit, I will give you such-and-such, and if I gain booty in my raid, I will make you a share. Al-Dahhak: Return to them a good response. It was also said: it is supplication. Ibn Zayd said: if he is not your child and not someone whose maintenance is obligatory for you, then say to him "a kind word": say to him, "May God keep us and you well; may God bless you." Al-Mufaddal said: a gentle word by which their souls are made content; whatever the soul is content with and loves, whether a word or deed, is ma'ruf (the recognized good); and whatever it denies, dislikes, and recoils from is munkar (the rejected evil).

﴿And test the orphans﴾ — the verse. It was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Rifa'ah and his paternal uncle. Rifa'ah died and left his son Thabit, who was young. Thabit's uncle came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My nephew is an orphan in my care; what is lawful for me from his wealth, and when should I give him his wealth?" So God revealed: ﴿And test the orphans﴾.

That is: examine them in their intellects and their bodies, and in their preservation of their wealth. ﴿Until they reach marriageable age﴾, that is, the age of men and women. ﴿And if you perceive (aanastum)﴾, that is, you see. God said: ﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the mount﴾ [[Surah al-Qasas: 29.]].

The poet said:
"I perceived a bird's cry, and the hunter frightened it, in the afternoon, when evening had drawn near."
[[Gharib al-Hadith li-Ibn Qutaybah: 1/22; Lisan al-'Arab: 1/164.]]

In the codex of 'Abd Allah: fa-in ahassatum, meaning ahsastum, so one of the two sins is dropped, like their saying: ﴿So you would have continued to be amazed﴾ [[Surah al-Waqi'ah: 65.]].

The poet said:
"Indeed the she-camels of the noble ones, they perceived it, and so they are fierce toward it."
[[al-Tibyan: 7/205; Taj al-'Arus: 4/128, attributed to Abu Zubayd.]]

﴿Sound judgment (rushdan)﴾ from them. The common reading is with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the shin. al-Sulami and 'Isa recited with a fatha on the ra' and the shin, and both are dialects.

The exegetes said: it means intellect, righteousness, preservation of wealth, and knowledge of what sets it right.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Sha'bi said: a man grasps his beard, and he has reached maturity; his wealth is not handed over to the orphan even if he is an old man, until his sound judgment is perceived.

Al-Dahhak said: the orphan is not given his wealth even if he reaches a hundred years, until it is known from him that he sets his wealth right.

Mention of the ruling of the verse:
Know that God made the lifting of restriction from the orphan minor, and the permissibility of handing over his wealth to him, conditional upon two things: puberty and sound judgment, after commanding the guardians to test them.

The meaning of testing, as some jurists have stated: the minor is not free from one of two states: either he is a boy or a girl. If he is a boy, the management of household expenses is returned to him for a month, or he is given a small amount to dispose of, so that it may be known how he manages and deals with it. If she is a girl, what is returned to the mistress of the house is returned to her: the management and oversight of her household, and in spinning, supervising the spinners regarding the distribution of cotton and its wages, and securing the thread and its quality. If they show sound judgment, well and good; otherwise they both remain under restriction until their sound judgment is perceived. [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/35.]]

As for puberty, it occurs through one of five causes: three shared by men and women, and two specific to women. The three shared: the wet dream, which is the emission of semen; whenever one of these occurs, he has reached puberty, whether it is from intercourse, a wet dream, or otherwise. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission﴾ [[Surah al-Nur: 59.]], and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Mu'adh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Take from every adult male a dinar, or its equivalent in Ma'afir cloth." [[Sunan Abi Dawud: 1/354, no. 1576.]] [239]

The scholars differed about this. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: when the boy completes fifteen years, or grows the hair, we judge that he has reached puberty.

Abu Hanifah said: if it is a girl, her puberty is seventeen years. As for the boy, there are two reports from him: one is nineteen years, which is the more well-known and the one relied upon. It is narrated from him by al-Lu'lu'i: eighteen years.

Malik and Dawud said: puberty is not reached by age. Then they differed: Dawud said: age does not make one reach puberty as long as he has not had a wet dream, even if he reaches forty years. Malik said: his puberty is when his voice becomes coarse or his nostrils split.

The evidence that the basis for puberty by age is fifteen years is the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, who said: I was presented to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the year of Uhud, and I was fourteen years old, and he turned me away, not seeing me as having reached maturity. I was presented to him in the year of the Trench, and I was fifteen years old, and he permitted me to join the fighting.

The growing of hair: that is, hair growing coarse around the private parts of a boy or a girl.

Al-Shafi'i has two positions on hair growth: first, that it is puberty; second, that it is an indication of puberty.

Abu Hanifah said: no ruling is attached to hair growth; it is neither puberty nor an indication of it.

The evidence that puberty by hair growth is connected to it is what 'Atiyyah al-Qurazi narrated from Sa'd ibn Mu'adh: that the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed him to judge the Banu Qurayzah. He said: "I kept examining them, and whoever had grown hair, I killed him, and whoever had not grown hair, I placed among the offspring." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You have judged by the judgment of God from above the seven heavens." [[Zad al-Masir: 6/194; al-Fa'iq of al-Zamakhshari: 2/52.]] [240]

Atiyya said: "So I was among those who had not grown hair, and He placed me among the offspring."

As for what is specific to women: menstruation and pregnancy. This is supported by what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The prayer of a menstruating woman is not accepted without a head-covering." [Musnad Ahmad: 4/150; Sunan Abi Dawud: 1/152, no. 641.] So he made her accountable (mukallafa) through menstruation, and this statement concerns the limit of puberty.

As for maturity of judgment (rushd), the jurists have differed concerning it. Al-Shafi'i said: it is that a person be upright in his religion (salih fi dinihi) and sound in managing his property (muslih fi malihi). Uprightness in religion means that he avoids the grave sins (fawahish) by which he commits transgression (yafsuqu) and which cause the loss of his integrity ('adala), such as fornication (zina), sodomy (liwat), slanderous accusation (qadhf), drinking wine, and the like. Sound management of property means that he does not squander it, does not waste it (tabdhir), and is not defrauded in his dealings with a gross deception (ghabn fahish). Thus rushd consists of two things: fitness to give testimony, and sound management of property. This is the view of al-Hasan, Rabi'a, and Malik.

Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: if he reaches puberty sensible and sound in managing his property, the restriction (hajr) is lifted from him in every case, whether he is corrupt in his religion or upright in it. They took account of soundness of property and did not take account of soundness of religion.

Then they differed concerning one who reaches puberty sensible but corrupt in managing his property:
Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: the restriction is not lifted from him, and his dispositions are void except for marriage and manumission; he remains under restriction forever until his maturity of judgment becomes evident.
Abu Hanifa said: if he reaches puberty sensible, the restriction is lifted from him; but if he is corrupt in managing his property, his property is withheld from being handed over to him until he reaches twenty-five years of age, and when he reaches it, the property is handed over to him in every case, whether or not he is corrupting it. It is said that during the period in which his property is withheld, when he reaches puberty corrupt, his dispositions take effect absolutely, and the withholding of the property from him is only out of caution for his property. He said: the reason for setting the limit at twenty-five years is that a man may father a child at twelve years, then have a child at six months of age, then his child may father a child at twelve years, then have a child at six months, and thus he becomes a grandfather.
He said: "I am ashamed to restrict one who is fit to be a grandfather." And when puberty and maturity of judgment are attained, the property is handed to him, whether or not he has married.

Malik said: if the owner of the property is a girl and she reaches maturity of judgment, the restriction remains upon her, and she is prevented from her property until she marries; when she marries, her property is handed over to her, but it is not permissible for her to dispose of her property without the permission of her husband until she grows older and is tested; then, at that point, her disposal without his permission is considered remote. As for the boy, it is absolute. What proves the corruption of this school is what is related: that the Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon on the day of the feast, then descended and went to the women and admonished them, saying: "Give charity, even from your jewelry." So they began to give charity, the woman casting off her ornaments out of eagerness and generosity. He (peace be upon him) commanded them to give charity and accepted it from them, and he did not distinguish between a married woman and an unmarried one, nor between one who gave charity with her husband's permission and one who did so without it.

This is the discussion of restriction on minors, and the explanation of the ruling of His words: "And test the orphans" (4:6). As for His words: "And do not give the foolish your property..." (4:5), the ruling concerning the discussion of restriction upon the foolish (safih) is as follows:

The scholars differed concerning it:
Abu Hanifa and a group said: there is no restriction upon a free, adult, sensible person in any way, even if he is the most corrupt of people and the most prodigal. This is the view of al-Nakha'i. They argued for this with what Qatada related from Anas: that Hayyan ibn Munqidh used to be deceived in sales, so his family came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Hayyan ibn Munqidh conducts transactions, and there is weakness in his transactions, so restrict him." So the Prophet (ﷺ) summoned him and said: "Do not sell." He said: "I cannot refrain from selling." So he said to him: "When you trade, say: 'No deception (la khalaba), and you have the option for three days.'" [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/27.]
When the people asked that he be restricted for the deception in his dealings and he did not do so, it was established that it is not permissible.

Al-Shafi'i said: if he corrupts his property and his religion, or corrupts his property but not his religion, he is restricted. If he corrupts his religion but manages his property soundly, there are two views:
The first: he is restricted; this is the opinion of Abu al-'Abbas ibn Surayj.
The second: he is not restricted; this is the opinion of Abu Ishaq al-Marwazi. The more apparent view of al-Shafi'i's school, and that which we have mentioned concerning restriction of the foolish, is the view of 'Uthman, 'Ali, al-Zubayr, 'A'isha, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far. Among the Successors (tabi'un) it was Shurayh, and among the jurists it was said by Malik, the people of Madina, al-Awza'i, the people of Syria, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Our companions claimed consensus (ijma') on this issue, and what is related by Hisham ibn 'Urwa from his father: that 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far bought a salty land for sixty thousand dirhams, was deceived in it, and 'Ali wanted to restrict him. So Ibn Ja'far went to al-Zubayr and said: "I have bought, and 'Ali wants to go to the rabbi of the believers and ask him to restrict me."
Al-Zubayr said: "I am your partner in the sale." He said: "Then 'Ali went to 'Uthman."
'Ali said: "Ibn Ja'far bought such-and-such; restrict him."
Al-Zubayr said: "I am his partner in the sale." 'Uthman said: "How can I restrict a man in a sale in which his partner is al-Zubayr?"
Thus from this account the consensus of the Companions on the permissibility of restriction is established, for 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far feared restriction, al-Zubayr devised a way to protect him from it, 'Ali asked 'Uthman for it, and 'Uthman excused himself from doing it.

"And do not consume them extravagantly" (4:6), O assemblies of guardians and trustees, "beyond what is right." Extravagance (israf) is exceeding the limit, excess, error, and placing a thing in other than its place. It is said: "I passed by you and was forgetful (sarraqtukum), i.e., I was heedless of you and missed you." Jarir said:
"Give Hunayda, which is driven by eight [camels],
there is in their giving neither favor (manna) nor excess (saraf)."
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/337.]
That is, error, meaning that they hit the right places of giving.

"And do not hasten (bidaran) to [spend it] before they grow up" (4:6): "an anticipating" (mubadara) "that they grow up" — the clause is in the accusative position; meaning: do not hasten their growing up and their maturity, lest they reach it and you become obliged to hand their property over to them. Then He clarified what is lawful for them from their property, so He, mighty and majestic, said: "And whoever is wealthy" from the property of the orphan, "let him abstain" (yastaʿfif) from the property of the orphan, so it is not permissible for him, little or much. Abstinence (ʿiffa) is refraining from what is not lawful and not finding it permissible to do. God Most High said: "And let those who do not find a marriage be chaste (yastaʿfif)" (24:33).

"And whoever is poor," needing the property of the orphan while he looks after it and attends to it, "let him eat according to what is reasonable (bil-maʿruf)." The scholars differed concerning it:
Some of them said: al-maʿruf is a loan, with the parallel of His words: "except one who enjoins charity or what is reasonable" (4:114), meaning a loan. The meaning of the verse: you borrow from the orphan's property, and when you become well-off you repay it; if you cannot repay it, there is nothing upon you.
This was held by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Abu al-'Aliya, and most of the reports from Ibn 'Abbas.
Mujahid said: he should borrow from it, trade with it, and when he becomes well-off he repays. The evidence for this interpretation is what Isra'il and Sufyan related from Ishaq from Haritha ibn Mudarrib, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Indeed, I have placed myself in relation to God's property in the position of an orphan's property: if I am rich I abstain, if I am poor I eat in a reasonable manner, and if I become well-off I repay."
Al-Sha'bi said: "Do not eat it except when you are compelled to, as you are compelled to eat carrion."
Others said: "bil-maʿruf" means that he eats it without extravagance and without owing anything for what he eats. Then they differed on the manner of this reasonable eating:
'Ata', 'Ikrima, and al-Suddi said: he eats with the tips of his fingers and does not exceed in eating, and he does not clothe himself with it.
al-Nakha'i said: he does not wear fine garments or linen, but only what satisfies hunger and covers nakedness.
Some said: it is that he eats from the fruit of his palms and the milk of his livestock in a reasonable manner, with no repayment owed; but gold and silver are not included, for if he consumes them he must return them. This is the view of al-Hasan and a group.
Qatada said: the orphan would have a garden of palm trees; his guardian would look after its upkeep and irrigation and take from its fruit, and he would have livestock; his guardian would look after their upkeep and care and take from their wool and their milk-yield; but as for the capital and roots of the property, he may not destroy them.
al-Dahhak said: "al-maʿruf" is riding the animal and having the servant serve, and he may not eat anything of his property.
Ibn Abi Najih related from al-Muhsin al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, I have an orphan in my care; shall I strike him?" He said: "As much as you would strike your own son." He said: "O Messenger of God, shall I eat from his property?" He said: "Reasonably, without accumulating wealth from his property and without protecting your property with his property."
The root of al-maʿruf is what is made easy for a person such that his soul is content with it. God Most High said: "a provision in accordance with what is reasonable" (2:241).

"And when you hand over their property to them, then call witnesses against them." This is a discipline from God Most High, so that it may be known that the guardian has discharged the trust, the suspicion is cut off from him, and dispute is removed; and it is not an obligation. "And God suffices as a reckoner" (4:6): one who calls to account, requites, and witnesses.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 4, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 3):

Madaniyya (Medinan), containing sixteen thousand and thirty letters, three thousand seven hundred and forty-five words and one hundred, and seventy-six verses.

On the authority of Abu Umama, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Nisa', it is as if he has given charity to every believer who has inherited an inheritance, and he is given a reward like one who has freed a slave, and he is free from shirk, and he is among those whom Allah may pardon." [Majma' al-Bayan: 3/5.] [225]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾ — meaning Adam — ﴿and created from it its mate﴾ — meaning Eve. Its parallel is in Surat al-A'raf and al-Zumar. ﴿And dispersed from the two of them many men and women.﴾ *Batha* means he spread and made manifest. ﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another﴾ — you ask one another by Him. The people of Kufa lightened it (*tasa'alun*) by dropping one of the two *ta'*s, as a lightening, like His saying: ﴿and do not cooperate﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 2] and similar. ﴿And the wombs.﴾

The common reading is with the accusative (*nasb*), meaning: ﴿and fear the wombs, lest you sever them.﴾

Al-Nakha'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talha ibn Musarrif, Qatada, al-A'mash and Hamza read it in the genitive (*khafd*), meaning *wa-bil-arham* (and by the wombs), as one says: "I ask you by Allah and the Merciful," and "I adjure you by Allah and the Merciful." The first reading is more correct and more eloquent, because the Arabs do not coordinate an apparent noun with a pronoun governed by a preposition, unless they repeat the governing particle, saying: "I passed by him and by Zayd," or they put it in the accusative, as in the words of the poet:

"O people, what is wrong with me and Abu Dhu'ayb?"

However, it is permissible with the aforementioned construction, and it occurs in poetry. The poet said:

"Today you have come near to satirizing us and insulting us... go, what have you to do with the days, [which are] a wonder?" [Sharh al-Radi 'ala al-Kafiya: 2/336; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/14.]

Al-Farra' recited for one of the Ansar:

"We hang our swords among the like of pillars, and between them and the ankle is a ... (mahwa / ghawt) of nafanif." [Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/300; al-Qurtubi: 5/3, where it reads *mahwa* instead of *ghawt*.]

Abdullah ibn Yazid al-Muqri' read ﴿wal-arhamu﴾ in the nominative, as if he intended the sentence to be complete at His saying ﴿you ask one another by Him﴾, and then began anew, as one says: "Zayd should be honoured." It may also be an exhortation (*igra'*), since the Arabs put the one being urged in the nominative.

Al-Farra' recited:

"Where are the people among whom is 'Umayr, and the likes of 'Umayr, and among them al-Saffah,
worthy of meeting when the champion of valour says: 'The weapons! The weapons!'" [Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/208; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/6.]

﴿Indeed Allah is ever watchful over you﴾ — i.e., a guardian. It is said: it means *fa'il* (one who watches).

﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ — the verse.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning a man from Ghatafan who had much property belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the orphan reached maturity he demanded the property, but his uncle refused him, so they went to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. When the uncle heard it, he said: "We obey Allah and we obey the Messenger; we seek refuge in Allah from the great sin," and he handed over his property to him.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul and obeys his Lord in this way, he will enter his abode," meaning his Paradise. When the young man received his property, he spent it in the way of Allah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The reward remains and the burden remains."

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we understand that the reward remains, but how does the burden remain, when he spent it in the way of Allah?"

He said: "The reward remains for the boy, and the burden remains upon his father." And ﴿give﴾ is an address to the guardians and executors of orphans. [Al-Qurtubi: 5/8; Asbab al-Nuzul: 94, with variation in wording.] [227]

As for His saying, ﴿the orphans﴾: they are no longer orphans after reaching maturity, but this is figurative usage, like His saying: ﴿and the sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾ [Surat al-A'raf: 120]. There were no sorcerers with the prostration, but they were named by what they had been before prostrating.

His saying: ﴿give the orphans their property﴾ means: those who were orphans, when they reach maturity ﴿and you perceive in them maturity of judgement﴾. Its parallel is: ﴿and test the orphans﴾ [Surat al-Nisa': 6]. ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ means: do not substitute their unlawful property that is upon you for your lawful property that is for you. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿The bad and the good are not equal﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 100].

They differed concerning the meaning and manner of this interpretation:

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: The guardians of orphans and their executors would take the good and choice from the orphans' property and put in its place the inferior and base, so one of them might take a fat sheep from the orphan's property and put in its place a lean sheep, and take a good dirham and throw in its place a counterfeit, and say: "A dirham for a dirham." That is their substitution, and Allah the Exalted forbade it.

Ata': "Do not profit at the expense of your orphan who is in your charge, while he is weak and young."

Ibn Zayd: The people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance to women and children, and the eldest would take the inheritance.

Ibn Zayd also said: ﴿and you desire to marry them, and the weak among the children﴾ — they did not give them any share of the inheritance; so their share of the inheritance is good, and this which they took is bad.

Mujahid and Badhan: "Do not hasten the unlawful provision before the lawful comes to you."

﴿And do not devour their property along with your property﴾ — i.e., together with your property, like His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers to Allah?﴾ [Surat Al 'Imran: 52; Surat al-Saff: 14].

Al-Mufaddal recited Salama ibn al-Kharashib al-Ansari:

"They close the doors of the tents with lean [horses] towards ... firmly fastened tendons (ankles/nawasir)." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/10; Lisan al-'Arab: 4/23.]

That is, together with *'unun*.

﴿Indeed it is a great sin﴾ — i.e., a grave wrong. In it there are three dialects: the common reading is *huban* with a *damma*, and it is the dialect of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the people of the Hijaz, as shown by what Abu 'Ubayd related from 'Abbad ibn 'Abbad, from Wasil, the client of Ibn 'Uyayna, who said: I said to Ibn Sirin: "How is this word read: *innahu kana hauban* or *haubā*?" He said: Abu Ayyub wished to divorce Umm Ayyub, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "The divorce of Umm Ayyub is a sin (*hawb*)." [al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 25/136.] [228]

al-Hasan read *haubā* with a fatha on the *ha'*, which is the dialect of Tamim.

[Muqatil said: the dialect of the Abyssinians.] [Addition from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/10.]

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read *hābā* as a verbal noun, like *al-qāl*, and it may be a noun like *al-rād* and *al-nār*. It is said that the sin is *hawb* and *hāb*, and so for the plural; it is both verbal noun and noun. It is said: *hāba yahūbu hawban* and *hawban* and *hibāyatan* when one sins.

Abu Mu'adh said: We alighted at a place near a city, and a man threw a small stone [and it was said to him]: "O pilgrim, do not kill it, lest you incur a sin (*hawb*); it does not harm." From this the killer is called *hā'ib*. Al-Farra' related it from the Banu Asad.

Umayya ibn al-Askan al-Laythi, whose son had emigrated without his permission, said:

"Even if two emigrants surround him that morning, they have erred and sinned (*hābā*)."
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/306.]

Another said:

"Bite on your molars, the shrewd one, so he does not blame nor sin (*yahūb*)."
[al-Fa'iq li-l-Zamakhshari: 2/180.]

Another said:

"And the son of her son from us and from you, and her husband Khuzayma, and the wombs, the distress of her sin (*hawbihā*)."
[Lisan al-'Arab: 2/202.]

That is, its sin is severe.

Another said:

"Do not weep for me, nor lament with the speech of sin; indeed sin is a grave wrong (*hawb*)."
[Tarikh Dimashq: 63/173.]

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with regard to the orphans﴾ — the verse. The exegetes differed concerning its revelation and interpretation. Some of them said: its meaning is: "And if you fear that you will not be just, O guardians of orphans, regarding them, when you marry them, then marry others besides them from the women whom Allah has made lawful to you."

Al-Zuhri related from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, who said: I asked her about the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with regard to the orphans﴾. She said: "O son of my brother, it refers to the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian, who desires her wealth and beauty and wishes to marry her for less than her dowry. They were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly towards them in completing the dowry, and they were ordered to marry other women besides them."

al-Hasan said: A man of Madina would have orphans in his care, and among them were some whom it was lawful for him to marry, but he would say to her: "I will not let anyone enter my property," out of dislike that a stranger should enter and share in their wealth. So he might marry them for the sake of their wealth, and [marry] one whom he does not find pleasing, then he forgets their companionship and waits for them to die so that he may inherit from them. Allah the Mighty and Majestic condemned that, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.

'Ikrima: A man of Quraysh would marry ten women, or more or less. When he became unable to meet the expenses of his wives, he would seize the property of his orphan ward in his care and spend it. So it was said to them: "Refrain from women, and do not exceed four, lest it lead you to take the property of orphans." This is the report of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the sense of the report of 'Ata' from him.

Others said: They would scruple and feel sinful regarding the property of orphans, and would be lax regarding women, not limiting themselves regarding them, and would marry as many as they wished, so that they were sometimes just and sometimes not. When they asked about the matter of the orphans' property, Allah revealed ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, and He also revealed this verse: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with regard to the orphans﴾, meaning: just as you fear not being just with the orphans and it preoccupies you, so likewise fear regarding women that you will not be just to them, and do not marry more than you can keep and fulfil their rights, for women are like the orphan in weakness and helplessness. How is it that you are conscientious towards Allah the Mighty and Majestic in one matter, yet disobey Him in its like? This is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, and the report of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

al-Hasan also said: They scrupled over marrying orphans as they scrupled over their property, so Allah revealed this verse, and granted leniency regarding them and restricted them to a number. So it is incumbent upon you to be just regarding them. If you fear, O guardians, regarding the orphans whose guardianship you hold, that you will not act justly, then marry them, but do not exceed four, so that you may be just; and if you fear that you will not be just regarding them, then one.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The men were restricted to four women because of the orphans.

Mujahid: its meaning is: if you scrupulously avoid the guardianship of orphans, then [scrupulously avoid] their property out of faith and belief; likewise be scrupulous about adultery, and marry lawful women in a good marriage. Then He specified for them a limited number, whereas they used to marry as many as they wished without any number. So Allah revealed ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾, i.e., that you will not be just.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read *tuqsitū* with a fatha on the *ta'*, which is also from justice.

al-Zajjaj said: *qasata* and *aqsata* are one; however, the more eloquent is *aqsata* when he is just, and *qasata* when he is unjust. If the reading of Ibrahim is taken to mean injustice, and *lā* is considered superfluous, the sentence is sound. *Al-yatama* is the plural of male orphans.

﴿So marry﴾ — *mā*.

Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ayla read *man* (مَن), because *mā* is for what does not reason and *man* for what reasons. Whoever reads *mā* has two aspects:

First: that it refers to the act, not the person, its meaning being: "marry the marriage which is lawful to you from women." This is like saying: "Take from my companion what you wish, and the brothers," making *mā* mean *man*. The Arabs interchange *mā* with *man* and *man* with *mā*.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿By the heaven and He who built it﴾ [Surat al-Shams: 5] and its like, and He said: ﴿Of them is one who walks on his belly﴾ [Surat al-Nur: 45].

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' related that the people of Makka, when they heard thunder, said: "Glory to Him whom the thunder glorifies." And Allah said: ﴿Pharaoh said: And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [Surat al-Shu'ara': 23].

﴿Good for you of women, two, three, or four﴾ — *tāba*, *ḥalla lakum min al-nisā'*.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Juhdari and al-A'mash read *tāba* with *imāla* (inclination of the vowel), and in the codex of Ubayy it is written *ṭayyib* with a *yā'*, which is evidence of *imāla*.

*Mathnā wa-thulātha wa-rubā'* are inflected away from two, three and four, and therefore are not declined. There are dialect forms: *muwaḥḥad, mathnā, muthallath, mirba'*, and *aḥād, thanā', thulātha, rubā'*, and *aḥad, thunā, thulth, rub'*, like *'Umar* and *Zufar*.

Likewise al-Nakha'i read this verse. No formation beyond four is used except one line from al-Kumayt:

"They did not ask you to pause until you had struck, above the men, qualities of ten (*'ishār*)."
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/316.]

That is, you struck ten.

They said: Here it means [*law* for affirmation] [The apparent reading is so.], as in His saying: ﴿I admonish you with one thing: that you stand up for Allah in pairs and singly﴾ [Surat Saba': 46], and His saying: ﴿Possessors of wings, two, three, and four﴾ [Surat Fatir: 1]. This is the consensus of the community, and the particular privileges of the Prophet (ﷺ) are not shared.

al-Kalbi, from Khumaisa bint al-Shamardal: Qays ibn al-Harith related to her that he had eight free wives. He said: When this verse was revealed, I said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has revealed to you the prohibition of marrying free women beyond four, and I have eight wives." He said: "Divorce four and keep four." He said: I returned to my house and began to say to the wife who had not borne me children: "O so-and-so, go back," and to the wife who had borne children: "O so-and-so, come forward." Then the one he divorced would say: "I adjure you by Allah and by affection." He said: So I divorced four and kept four. [Abridged, Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/628, hadith 1952.]

﴿And if you fear﴾ — you feared, and it is said: you knew — ﴿that you will not act justly﴾ among the four — ﴿then one﴾.

The common reading is with the accusative (*naṣb*).

al-Hasan, al-Juhdari and Abu Ja'far read *wāḥidatun* with the nominative, meaning: let one suffice you, i.e., one that is sufficient, like His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and if there are not two men, then a man and two women﴾ [Surat al-Baqara: 282].

﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾ — meaning the slave-girls and concubines, because you are not bound towards them by the rights and duties that bind you in regard to marriage; there is no division of time for you among them, and no limit upon you regarding their number. Mention of "right hands" is an explanation of the sense: *aw mā malakat*.

Some scholars of meaning said: *aw mā malakat aymānukum* means: that which your divisions (*aqsām*) take effect upon; he took it from the oath of swearing, not the oath of the limb, and he argued by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no vow in disobedience to Allah, nor in what the son of Adam does not possess." [al-Sunan al-Kubra: 10/33; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/711.] [230]

﴿That is nearer﴾ — closer — ﴿that you will not commit excess (*ta'ūlū*)﴾.

From Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, from 'A'isha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿That is nearer that you will not commit excess﴾, he said: "That you will not act unjustly." [Fath al-Qadir: 1/424.] [231]

Hisham ibn 'Urwa also related from 'A'isha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿That is nearer that you will not commit excess﴾ — that you will not deviate. Most exegetes hold this view.

Muqatil said: It is the dialect of Jurhum; it is said: *mīzān 'ā'il*, meaning a leaning scale. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to the people of Kufa concerning something they had reproached him for: "I am not a scale that leans (*lā u'ūl*)."

'Ikrima recited for Abu Talib:

"With a scale of truth that does not shortchange a grain, having a witness from itself, not leaning."
[Lisan al-'Arab: 11/489; al-Sihah of al-Jawhari: 5/1777.]

Mujahid said: That is nearer that you will not go astray. Al-Farra' and al-Asamm said: that you will not exceed what Allah has obligated upon you; the root of *'awl* is excess, and from it comes *'awl al-farā'id* (the increase in shares of inheritance). al-Shafi'i said: that you will not have many dependants. No one said this except him. It is said: *a'āla yu'īlu* when his dependants increase. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/22, which mentions that al-Daraqutni and Jabir ibn Yazid adopted this opinion.]

Abu Hatim said: [al-Shafi'i] was more knowledgeable in the language of the Arabs than we are, and perhaps this is a dialect.

al-Tha'labi said: Our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: I asked Abu 'Amr al-Duri about this, and he was an unchallenged imam in language. He said: It is the dialect of Himyar.

And he recited:

"Indeed death seizes every living being, without doubt, even if he walks [with many] and has many dependants (*'ālā*)."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/22.]

That is, his flocks and dependants increased.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: The Arab tongues have multiplied so much that I fear I will take a solecism from a speaker of error.

Talha ibn Musarrif read *allā ta'ūlū* (*ta'ūlū*, from *i'āla*), which is the strength of al-Shafi'i's opinion. Some read *allā ta'ūlū* from *al-'ayla*, i.e., not to become poor.

The poet said:

"The poor man does not know when he will become wealthy, and the wealthy man does not know when he will become poor (*yu'īl*)."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/106.]

Tawus read *lā ta'ūlū*, from *al-'illa* (the ailment).

Bashir ibn Nahik related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has two wives and inclines towards one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of him leaning." [Sunan Abi Dawud: 1/473; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/341.] [232]

﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾ (*nihla*).

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 4, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Kalbi and a group of scholars said: this is addressed to the guardians (awliya'). The guardian of a woman, when he married her to a stranger, would carry her to him on a camel and would give her nothing of her dowry (mahr). If she was among her own tribe, he would not give her any of her dowry, little or much. If she was a stranger, he would carry her on a camel to her husband and give her nothing beyond that camel.

For this reason they used to say to a man who had a daughter born to him: "Congratulations on the nafijah [[al-nafijah: one who enlarges her father's wealth; cited in al-Sihah, 1/345.]]." They meant that he takes her dowry in camels and adds them to his camels, so he swells them (yanfajuha), that is, he enlarges and increases them.

Some women said of their husband:
"He does not take the bribe (hulwan) from his daughters."
She meant: he does not do what others do. So God, Mighty and Majestic, forbade them from this and commanded them to give the right (haqq) to its people.

Al-Hadrami said: the guardians of women used to give one man's sister in exchange for the other man giving his sister, with no dowry between them. They were forbidden from this, and God commanded them to name the dowry and to specify the mahr at the contract.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no shighar (exchange-marriage) in Islam." [[Sahih Muslim: 4/139; Musnad Ahmad: 4/441.]] [233]

Others said: the address is to the husbands, who were commanded to give their wives their dowries, which are the price of their private parts (furuj). This view is more sound and clearer in the apparent meaning of the verse, and closer to it, because God addressed the marrying parties in what precedes it, and this is the basic form of address. The word sadaqat (dowries) is the plural of sadaqah, pronounced with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal in the plural form; this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Tamim. Some say sadaqah with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal. When they pluralize it they say sadaqat with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal, and sadaqat with a damma on both, like zulmah and zulumat. Zulumat has as its counterpart al-mathulat (plural of mathulah), the dialect of Tamim being mathulah and mathulat, and mathulat with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha', its singular being mathulah, in the plural form, the dialect of the Hijaz.

Nihlatan: Qatadah said: an obligatory duty (fari'dah wajibah). Ibn Juraij and Ibn Zayd said: a specified duty (fari'dah musammah). Abu 'Ubayd said: a nihlah cannot be specified and known. Al-Kalbi said: a gift and a grant. Abu 'Ubaydah said: from a willing soul (an tayyib nafs). Al-Zajjaj said: as a religious obligation (tadayyun). In it there are two dialects: nihlah and nahlah. Its origin is from giving, and it is in the accusative as a specification (tafsir), and it was said it is an infinitive (masdar).

Marthad ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The most worthy of conditions to be fulfilled is that by which you have made the private parts lawful for you." [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/144; Musnad Abi Ya'la: 2/291.]] [234]

And from Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ziyad ibn Suhayb, from his father, from his grandfather Suhayb, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes on a debt while intending not to repay it will meet God, Mighty and Majestic, as a thief; and whoever gives a woman a dowry while intending not to pay it to her will meet God, Mighty and Majestic, as an adulterer." [[al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 8/35; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/322, no. 44724.]] [235]

﴿And if they are pleased to give you of it something willingly﴾ — meaning: if their souls are content to give you something of that, and they gift it to you. The verb is thus shifted from the souls to their owners, so the soul is an explicit specification (tamyiz). That is why "nafs" is singular, as one says: "He was constricted by it in measure (dharʿan)" and "his eye was cooled by it," and God says: ﴿and he was distressed on their account, and his heart was constricted﴾ [[Surah al-'Ankabut: 33.]].

Some grammarians of Kufa said: its wording is singular but its meaning is plural, and the Arabs do this often.

The poet said:
"Therein are the carcasses of the exhausted; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are hard."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/325.]]

Another said:
"In your throats there is a bone, and we have been choked by it."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/325.]]

Some grammarians of Basra said:
"When the night draws near, the lover's desire ..."
[[al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 10/225.]]
Here al-hawa (desire) is a masdar, and masdars are not pluralized.

﴿Then eat it﴾ means: take it and accept it. ﴿with ease and pleasure﴾ (hanian mariyan). Al-Hadrami said: some people used to feel sinful about a man taking back anything of what he had given to his wife, so God said: ﴿And if they are pleased to give you of it something willingly﴾, without compulsion or deception, ﴿then eat it with ease and pleasure﴾, meaning: pleasant and good. It is derived from the word hanna't al-ba'ir (the mange-treatment of a camel), when one treats it with tar for mange. The meaning is: eat it, healing and free from harm. Hana'ani al-ta'am yahnini (food made me comfortable) with the fatha on the nun in the past tense and kasra in the future tense, yahniini and yahnani, which is the opposite and is rare. The masdar of both is hana'un; one says: hana'ani and mara'ani without the alif. When they use them separately they say amra'ani with an alif. It was also said: al-hanii is the good enjoyment that nothing disturbs, and al-mari' is one whose outcome is praised, complete in digestion, harmless and not injurious. The meaning is: you will not fear in this world any demand, nor in the Hereafter any consequence.

This is supported by what Jawaybir narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he was asked about this verse, ﴿And if they are pleased to give you of it something willingly﴾, and he said: "If she gives her husband a gift willingly, not under compulsion, no authority will judge against you concerning it, and God will not hold you accountable for it in the Hereafter." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 5/27.]] [236]

Ibrahim ibn 'Isa narrated from 'Ali ibn 'Ali, from Abu Hamzah, who said: "hanian" means there is no sin in it, "mari'an" means there is no reckoning for it in the Hereafter.

Shu'bah narrated from 'Ali, who said: "If one of you is afflicted with something, let him ask his wife for three dirhams of her dowry, then buy honey with it, and drink it with rainwater; then God will gather for him the pleasant and wholesome, the healing, and the blessed water."

﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth which God has made for you a means of support﴾ — the verse.

They differed about who these foolish ones are.

Some people said: they are the women.

Al-Hadrami said: a man deliberately gave his wealth to his wife, and she placed it in other than what is right, so God revealed this verse.

Mujahid said: He forbade men from giving women their wealth, and he specified the foolish ones as being those who were wives, or were daughters, or were mothers.

Jawaybir narrated from al-Dahhak: women are among the most foolish of the foolish. This interpretation is supported by what 'Ali ibn Zayd narrated from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the Fire was created only for the foolish," he said it three times, "and indeed the foolish are women, except a woman who obeys her guardian." [[We have not found this hadith in this wording.]] [237]

Aban narrated from Ibn 'Ayyash, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: a black woman, bold in speech and sharp-tongued, came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "May my father and mother be sacrificed for you, O Messenger of God, say something good about us once, for it has reached me that you say all kinds of evil about us." He said: "What did you say to us?" She said: "You called us the foolish in His Book and you called us the deficient." He said: "Is it not enough deficiency that each of you leaves prayer for five days every month? Does it not suffice one of you that when she becomes pregnant she has the reward of one who guards the frontier in the path of God, and when she gives birth she is like one who is rolling in his blood in the path of God, and when she nurses, for every sip she has the reward of freeing a slave from the descendants of Isma'il, and when she stays awake, for every wakeful night she has the reward of freeing a slave from the descendants of Isma'il? That belongs to the believing women who are humble, patient, and who do not deny their husbands." [[238]] The black woman said: "How great a virtue, were it not for the condition that follows it." [[Majma' al-Bayan: 3/18.]]
